turns.instruction: Match a US ZIP code: exactly five digits and nothing else.
turns.user:
Task: Match a US ZIP code: exactly five digits and nothing else.

Write a pattern that matches exactly the strings that should match.

Must match:
  '00000'
Must not match:
  '1234'
turns.thinking: Using '+' would accept any length, which the fixed length rules out. Pattern: \d{5}

turns.instruction: Now match the digit strings that rule rejects on length: all-digit strings that are one to four digits, or six or more.
turns.user:
Task: Now match the digit strings that rule rejects on length: all-digit strings that are one to four digits, or six or more.

Write a pattern that matches exactly the strings that should match.

Must match:
  '1234'
Must not match:
  'abcde'
turns.thinking: The rejected lengths fall either side of five, so this is two branches: one to four digits, or six and above. Pattern: \d{1,4}|\d{6,}

turns.instruction: We are going international. Generalise the original rule to a postal code of any length from four to ten digits.
turns.user:
Task: We are going international. Generalise the original rule to a postal code of any length from four to ten digits.

Write a pattern that matches exactly the strings that should match.

Must match:
  '1234567890'
Must not match:
  '123'
turns.thinking: One bounded quantifier replaces the fixed count from the original rule. Pattern: \d{4,10}
